title: AI Buildout Overtakes Housing as America's Top Investment Engine
excerpt: Real spending on data centers and computer hardware hit $752 billion in the second quarter, surpassing residential investment for the first time — a milestone that shows where the economy's confidence now sits.
body:
• Inflation-adjusted spending on information-processing equipment — data centers, servers and computer hardware — reached an annualized $752 billion in the second quarter of 2026, edging past real private residential fixed investment of $748 billion, according to Fortune's analysis of Bureau of Economic Analysis data.
  • It is a historic reversal: spending on computing hardware is up 51% since early 2021, while residential investment is down 18% from its early-2021 peak.
  • Adam Shapiro, a vice president at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, called it "a pivotal shift" in the U.S. economy: "investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers."
  • Hyperscalers' AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year soon, even as the 30-year mortgage rate sits near 7% and the 10-year Treasury yield hits its highest since 2007.

The U.S. economy just crossed a line that economists will be quoting for years. In the second quarter of 2026, inflation-adjusted spending on information-processing equipment — the data centers, servers and computer hardware powering the artificial intelligence boom — reached an annualized $752 billion, according to Fortune's analysis of Bureau of Economic Analysis data. That edged past real private residential fixed investment of $748 billion. For most of modern American history, housing was the heavyweight investment category that shaped jobs, tax bases, mortgage markets and household wealth. The marginal dollar now flows to servers and power-hungry buildings built for AI.

Two booms, two decades apart

The symmetry is hard to miss. Two decades after the housing boom reshaped — and then nearly wrecked — the U.S. economy, a different boom is transforming its growth drivers. Meanwhile the housing market has been largely frozen since the COVID-era boom ended in 2022, when the Federal Reserve began its aggressive rate-hiking campaign to rein in inflation. A 30-year mortgage rate near 7% has frozen buyers and builders alike, and locked existing homeowners into the cheap loans they already hold. Construction spending tells the same story from the ground up: housing analyst Lance Lambert has documented data-center construction spending rising from about $25 for every $1,000 spent on new single-family homebuilding in 2022 to roughly $122 per $1,000 by April 2026.

Adam Shapiro, a vice president at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, flagged the milestone in a public LinkedIn analysis: "We're seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers. The AI investment boom is massive." His underlying point is about sensitivity to borrowing costs. Residential investment lives and dies by rates; AI capital spending has so far powered through them. The largest technology companies are converting capital into compute as fast as utilities, chip suppliers, power connections and local permits will allow — and they are increasingly borrowing to do it. Google parent Alphabet reported negative cash flow earlier this year, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has highlighted how eagerly AI companies are issuing debt no matter the cost of borrowing.

"We're seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers."

— Adam Shapiro, Vice President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

What it means for the real economy

The numbers underneath the milestone are blunt. Since early 2021, real spending on information-processing equipment has soared 51%, while residential fixed investment has fallen 18%. That tells you where business confidence has moved — and where it has not. Construction hiring, local tax receipts and household wealth formation still lean heavily on housing, which means the sector's stagnation continues to drag on large parts of the economy even as data-center projects lift industrial construction in a handful of regions. The $4 billion gap between the two categories is also narrow enough that a single quarter could flip it back; this is a signal about direction, not a settled verdict.

The concentration is the risk. A handful of hyperscalers accounts for the bulk of the AI buildout, with total spending projected to approach $1 trillion a year soon. If the returns on that capital spending disappoint — or if credit markets tighten — the economy's new growth engine is narrower than the housing market it displaced. For now, though, the buildout has become too large to treat as an ordinary tech cycle. It is the economy's story, and the investment data just made that official.

What's next

The test is durability. Watch whether hyperscaler capital expenditure keeps climbing into 2027 regardless of rates, whether power and permitting bottlenecks cap the buildout, and whether housing gets any relief if mortgage rates ease. The next quarterly investment data will show whether the crossover holds — or widens into a lasting new order.

nri_angle: Indian-Americans are heavily represented in the technology sector driving this buildout, from hyperscaler engineering teams to data-center construction and semiconductor supply chains, making the shift a direct read on the industry many in the community work in.
